text: The 1950s here arrive as a set rather than a period: a Manhattan block assembled from leather jackets, bad light and men who hold a pose until somebody looks. Suze and Arthur have been married a short while when a killing happens in front of them, and the aftershock sends them not to the police but into an argument with themselves. The greaser gang that takes an interest in the couple does not lose it. Kramer spends ninety-six minutes on that pressure, and she lets the film slide out of marital quarrel into something nearer a musical number, so that the question of who wants what is put into movement and costume before anyone says it aloud. Fantasy is listed among the genres, which is fair: the street is a stage, and the two of them are learning their blocking on it.

Two people talk, discover how much they have in common, and grow less comfortable with every minute of it. The film runs sixteen minutes and is filed as a thriller, which seems like a misfiling until the danger in the room comes into focus. Its subject is actors, people whose work is to be someone else, and the symmetry in what these two say starts to look less like coincidence than like a script neither will admit to holding. Seo Bo-hyung keeps the exchange close and unhurried. Agreement is usually a relief; here it accumulates like evidence. Sixteen minutes is too short to build suspense out of incident, so the suspense is built instead out of a suspicion: that what a person calls a self may have been assembled from parts of roles already played.

Accountancy is a shrewd profession to hand a man who is about to lose control of his own arithmetic. Jacquot puts one such man between two sisters, by accident rather than appetite, and then refuses to play any of it as farce. There is no villain, no fourth party, nobody who planned a thing. That is what makes a hundred minutes uneasy: almost every scene carries information that somebody standing in it does not have. The strain falls less on desire than on the bond between the sisters, which was in place long before he was, and which neither of them can renegotiate without the other noticing. Romance is the listed genre and it is accurate the way a barometer is accurate — the reading climbs, the air changes, and the people concerned go on discussing something else.

One bank in Paris stays open on Bastille Day, which is the whole idea, and the idea is the soundest thing in the film. Zed comes over from America with a single skill, opening vaults, and no plan of his own; Eric, an old friend, supplies the plan, the crew and the heroin, in roughly that order of enthusiasm. What follows first is not a heist but a night out — bars, music, a woman named Zoe who has been paid to be in the room — the kind of preamble most crime pictures compress into a montage. Avary lets it run. By the time the job starts, the men supposed to be professionals have been shown at length to be unfit for it, and ninety-six minutes leaves nobody time to sober up. The robbery is staged as a hangover: loud, badly lit, thoroughly earned.

A man rides a long way to sit at a table with someone he has not seen in twenty-five years, and neither of them says plainly why. Half an hour is an odd length for a western. It rules out what the genre usually spends its time on — the ride, the posse, a town slowly finding its nerve — and leaves the visit: a house, a meal, a night, a morning in which one man wears a badge and the other's gun work is spoken of in the past tense. Almodóvar keeps the pair indoors and close. What they once were to each other is not withheld for a late reveal; it is on the table early, and then has to be survived at close quarters, in daylight, a short walk from other people's windows. Thirty-one minutes, and much of the pressure comes from the fact that one of them has a job in that town tomorrow.

A refugee and a homeless punk fall in with each other in Berlin, and the first thing that has to be settled is where they will sleep. Dörrie takes 108 minutes over questions of that order: whose name can go on a document, who can be asked for a favour without a debt forming, what has to be said to whom to get through a winter. Neither has an address that an institution will accept, and that single fact organises everything after it, so the film lives in small permissions — a room, a bed, a signature, work that someone else can withdraw. Berlin here is less scenery than paperwork. Drama is the only genre listed, and the plainness is accurate. Tenderness is not offered as a reward for hardship; it is one more thing that must be arranged, guarded and paid for.

Fania tells her son stories, and the stories are more habitable than the rooms they are told in. Jerusalem in the years before there is a state, filmed at the height of a boy who is permitted to hear adult conversation and not to follow it. Portman stays at that height for most of ninety-five minutes: Arieh with his footnotes and his corrections, Fania whose inventions are not decoration but a method of getting through an afternoon, and a marriage in which only one of the two means every word literally. Politics enters as noise from the next street and as adults dropping their voices. The film is less interested in how a boy turns into a writer than in what it costs the person who has to keep supplying the household with stories, night after night, with the windows shut.

The van has a broken tail light, a detail that quietly decides how a trip like this goes once anyone in uniform is behind it. Five teenagers out of inland Oregon, school finished, set off for a Pacific coast none of them has seen, five hundred miles away, and that is the entire plan; they put it in two words themselves. A determined driver could manage the distance in a day. Ross takes a hundred and eleven minutes, which is the arrangement: the ocean is a direction rather than a destination, and the hours go on filling the tank, on people met at the side of the road, on the subject none of them raises directly, which is what happens after. They are at the age when friendship is still the main institution in a person's life. Having no plan, then, is not bravado but an accurate report of conditions.

A nineteen-year-old is moved into the adult wing ahead of schedule, and his father is already living on it. The film took the European Film Award for Best Sound Designer, and the credit is not ornamental: most of what Eric learns about his position arrives as noise from somewhere he cannot see — a door on a landing above, his name called down a corridor, a room going quiet when he walks in. Mackenzie gives him two available futures, neither dignified: the politics of the wing, which his father has spent years learning, or a circle of folding chairs run by a volunteer therapist with no power to protect anybody. A hundred and six minutes, nearly all of it indoors. The hardest thing in it is not the violence but the courtesy, the elaborate manners men keep up while working out which of them has to be hurt.
